events.title: Columbus reaches Cuba and Borinquen
events.summary: On his first voyage Columbus landed on Cuba, which he named Juana, on 28 October 1492; on his second, his fleet sighted Borinquen on 17 November 1493 and made landfall on its western coast on 19 November, naming it San Juan Bautista.
account: On the first voyage, after the Bahamas, Columbus headed toward the eastern coast of a large island he called Juana, present-day Cuba, landing there on 28 October 1492, and explored its northeast coast. In 1515 the name Juana was replaced by Fernandina.

The second voyage's fleet sighted the eastern coast of Puerto Rico, known to the Taíno as Borinquen, on the afternoon of 17 November 1493, sailed along its southern coast for a day, and made landfall on its northwestern coast at the Bay of Añasco, between Mayagüez and Aguadilla, early on 19 November. Columbus christened the island San Juan Bautista and remained anchored there on 20 and 21 November, sailing on to Hispaniola on 22 November.

Columbus returned to Cuba on 30 April 1494 and explored its south coast, which he believed to be a peninsula of China. The Taíno occupied the Greater Antilles; Hispaniola and Puerto Rico were the home of the Classic Taíno, and Cuba, Jamaica and the Bahamas of the Western Taíno.

events.title: Ponce de León conquers Borinquen and parcels out the Taíno
events.place: Caparra and San Juan Bay, Puerto Rico
events.summary: In 1508 Juan Ponce de León led the first official Spanish expedition to Puerto Rico, founded Caparra, became governor in 1509 and parcelled out the Taíno among the settlers in encomienda to mine gold and grow food.
account: Ponce de León had first seen the island on Columbus's second voyage in 1493 and had helped crush a Taíno rebellion on Hispaniola. In 1508 Ferdinand II of Aragon gave him permission for the first official expedition to the island the Spanish called San Juan Bautista; about 50 men in one ship left Hispaniola on 12 July 1508 and anchored in San Juan Bay, and placer gold was found in the west of the island. Archival documents suggest an earlier, quieter expedition as early as 1506.

He built a storehouse and fortified house about two miles from the bay, the first settlement, Caparra, in late 1508; it is a U.S. National Historic Landmark, the oldest known European settlement in the United States. Ovando appointed him governor, confirmed by Ferdinand II on 14 August 1509, with instructions to extend the settlement and continue mining for gold.

Ponce de León parcelled out the native Taínos among himself and other settlers under the forced-labour system of encomienda, putting them to work growing food and mining gold; his own encomienda searched for gold in the Toa Valley. Many Spaniards treated the Taínos very harshly and death rates were very high, and the demand for slaves kidnapped from other islands grew. By June 1511 the Taínos began a rebellion, put down by Ponce de León with crossbows and arquebuses. A 1530 story from Caparra tells of two Spaniards each with 40 Taíno slaves searching the rivers for gold.

events.title: Velázquez conquers Cuba; the massacre at Caonao
events.place: Baracoa, Bayamo, Caonao (Camagüey) and Havana, Cuba
events.summary: Diego Velázquez sailed from Hispaniola in January 1511 with about 300 men, defeated the Taíno resistance, founded Baracoa and six more towns by 1515, and apportioned the Native people in encomienda; Las Casas witnessed the massacre of the people of Caonao.
account: Las Casas estimated the Taíno population of Cuba at 350,000 by the end of the 15th century. Velázquez sailed for Cuba in January 1511 with four ships and 300 men, among them Hernán Cortés and Pedro de Alvarado, and landed in the province of Mayci. The Taínos, organized by the cacique Hatuey, were outmatched by Spanish weapons and defeated after two months of intermittent fighting. Baracoa was founded by August 1511, and Pánfilo de Narváez brought thirty Spanish archers and Native auxiliaries from Jamaica; within three years the Spanish controlled the island.

Las Casas observed a number of massacres, notably near Camagüey of the inhabitants of Caonao: by his account some three thousand villagers who had come to greet the Spanish with food were "without provocation, butchered". Survivors fled to the mountains or small islands before being captured and forced into reservations such as Guanabacoa.

In 1513 Ferdinand II decreed the encomienda system, and Velázquez apportioned the land and the Indigenous peoples among the colonists. Bayamo was founded in 1513 and Trinidad, Sancti Spíritus and Havana in 1514; gold deposits set off a gold rush until about 1520. The native population was largely destroyed as a culture after 1550; under the New Laws of 1552 Indigenous Cubans were freed from encomienda.

events.title: Cuba's sugar boom and the slave trade that outlived its ban
events.place: Havana, Santiago de Cuba and the sugar districts of western Cuba
events.summary: After the British occupation of Havana in 1762 and the Haitian Revolution, Cuba became one of the world's largest sugar producers on enslaved African labour; more than a million Africans were brought to the island, and the trade went on until 1867, decades after Spain agreed to end it.
account: Since the 1550s the Spaniards had relied on the Taíno for enslaved labour; as the Indigenous population declined from disease and warfare they introduced the chattel slavery of West Africans. Just over 40,000 enslaved people had been imported to the island in the 250 years before 1762.

In 1762 British forces under the Earl of Albemarle captured Havana and, during a year-long occupation, expanded the plantation system and imported 4,000 enslaved people from the British West Indies. Santiago de Cuba was authorized from 1789 as a port of arrival for the transatlantic trade. After the Haitian Revolution, Cuba's planters took much of the sugar market formerly held by Saint-Domingue and greatly expanded their imports from Africa: between 1791 and 1805, 91,211 enslaved people entered through Havana.

An Anglo-Spanish treaty of 1817 gained Spain's agreement to end the trade north of the Equator, but 372,449 enslaved people were imported before the trade legally ended and at least 123,775 between 1821 and 1853; lax enforcement brought an estimated 90,000 from 1856 to 1860. The Cuban trade continued until 1867. In all, more than a million enslaved Africans were brought to Cuba, from over 20 African peoples, chief among them Lucumí (Yoruba), Mandingo, Ganga, Arará, Carabalí and Congo.

On the sugar plantations, work days lasted close to 20 hours at harvest; the enslaved were locked at night in barracoons, put in stocks for days or months, and whipped, pregnant women included. The Spanish Black Code of 1789 limited lashings to 25, but planters flouted it.

events.title: The Aponte conspiracy
events.place: Havana, Puerto Príncipe (Camagüey), Bayamo and Holguín, Cuba
events.summary: In 1811–1812 the free black carpenter and militia corporal José Antonio Aponte of Havana organized an island-wide conspiracy to end slavery in Cuba; it was crushed, and Aponte was hanged on 9 April 1812, his head displayed in an iron cage.
account: As slavery expanded in Cuba at the beginning of the 19th century to take Haiti's place as the major sugar producer, a series of conspiracies against it followed; the first was discovered at Bayamo in 1795, headed by the freedman Nicolás Morales. In 1811 in Havana a new abolitionist conspiracy was organized by the freedman José Antonio Aponte, a first corporal in Havana's black militia of Yoruba origin, with reach to Sancti Spíritus, Trinidad, Camagüey, Bayamo, Holguín and Santiago. Hilario Herrera, a Dominican, tied the western conspiracy to the east.

The movement struck several sugar plantations outside Havana in March 1812 but was soon crushed. In Holguín more than 50 people were apprehended and the local leader, Juan Nepomuceno, from the Congo, was hanged. Hundreds of the enslaved were arrested and many leaders were tried and executed.

Aponte, convicted with eight of his companions on the evidence of his book of drawings, was hanged on 9 April 1812; he was then decapitated, his head placed in an iron cage in front of the house where he lived and his hand displayed on another street.

events.title: The Royal Decree of Graces settles Puerto Rico with Europeans
events.summary: On 10 August 1815 Ferdinand VII granted free land and incentives to Spaniards and other Catholic Europeans to settle Puerto Rico, to build a loyal population and a plantation economy worked by enslaved Africans and poor jornaleros; it 'whitened' the island into the 1850s.
account: On 10 August 1815 King Ferdinand VII approved a royal decree of graces opening Puerto Rico to trade with countries in good standing with Spain and granting free land and incentives to Spaniards willing to settle. An earlier decree of 1789 had granted Spanish subjects the right to purchase slaves and to take part in the transatlantic slave trade.

By 1825 Spain had lost all its American possessions but Puerto Rico and Cuba. Fearing the native-born mixed-race criollos would follow Haiti and the mainland into independence, the Crown revived the decree and distributed it across Europe to attract settlers who would be more loyal, on condition of loyalty to the Crown and allegiance to the Roman Catholic Church. Corsicans, Italians, French, Portuguese, Irish, Scots, Germans and others came from 1830 onward.

The settlers built sugarcane, coffee and tobacco plantations on enslaved African labour and needy jornaleros. The decree attracted many European immigrants, in effect 'whitening' the island into the 1850s; heavy immigration swelled the population to about one million by the end of the century, decreasing the proportion of Africans. Spain abolished the slave trade to its colonies on 25 June 1835, but slavery was not abolished in Puerto Rico until 1873.

events.title: Sugar slavery in Puerto Rico: Marcos Xiorro's conspiracy and Prim's Bando
events.summary: As sugar and slavery grew in 19th-century Puerto Rico, the enslaved conspired and revolted more than twenty times; in 1821 Marcos Xiorro planned a revolt against the planters, and on 31 May 1848 Governor Juan Prim imposed the Bando contra la Raza Africana to control all black Puerto Ricans, free or enslaved.
account: In the 19th century Spain established and expanded sugar cane production in Puerto Rico, and slavery increased. By 1873 the enslaved had carried out more than twenty revolts, some of great political importance, such as the Ponce and Vega Baja conspiracies.

In July 1821 the enslaved Marcos Xiorro planned and conspired to lead a revolt against the sugar planters and the Spanish colonial government. The conspiracy was suppressed, but Xiorro achieved legendary status among the enslaved and is part of Puerto Rico's heroic folklore.

Planters, nervous at the number of the enslaved, ordered restrictions on their movement; black Puerto Ricans were made to carry a notebook, the libreta, to move around the island. On 31 May 1848 Governor Juan Prim, fearing an independence or slave revolt, imposed draconian laws, the Bando contra la Raza Africana, to control the behaviour of all black Puerto Ricans, free or enslaved. Juan de la Pezuela replaced Prim that same year. In the Grito de Lares of 1868, free blacks who resented the libreta system burned their notebooks.

events.title: Triunvirato and La Escalera: the Year of the Lash
events.summary: After a series of slave revolts in 1843, led at the Triunvirato plantation by the Yoruba women Carlota and Fermina, the Spanish authorities claimed to uncover La Escalera, a conspiracy to end slavery, and answered with a terror in which thousands of Afro-Cubans, enslaved and free, were executed, imprisoned or banished.
account: In March, May and November 1843 a series of slave revolts occurred in Cuba. On 5 November 1843 the enslaved of the Triunvirato sugar mill in Matanzas rose, led by the African-born Lucumí women Carlota and Fermina with Eduardo, Narciso and Felipe Lucumí and Manuel Gangá; the revolt spread to the neighbouring Acaná estate and reached five plantations. Fermina had been whipped and kept in iron shackles for five months for running away. Carlota died in battle at the end of the revolt.

In December 1843 an enslaved woman, Polonia Gangá, told her master his property was about to be overtaken, and the authorities turned to stopping what they called the Conspiración de La Escalera, an alleged plot to abolish slavery. The British consul David Turnbull, already expelled, was convicted in absentia as its 'prime mover'. Historians have debated whether the conspiracy was real; there now seems to be a consensus that some revolt was planned.

The repression is called the Year of the Lash (Año del Cuero). La Escalera, 'the ladder', alludes to suspects being bound to ladders and whipped during interrogation. Thousands of Afro-Cubans, enslaved and free, were executed, imprisoned or banished; on 29 June 1844 a firing squad in Havana executed accused leaders. In 1912 Pedro Ivonnet of the Independent Party of Color called his party's exclusion "the epilogue of the trial of la Escalera."

events.title: El Grito de Lares
events.place: Lares and San Sebastián del Pepino, Puerto Rico
events.summary: On 23 September 1868 some 400–600 rebels of the Revolutionary Committee of Puerto Rico took Lares and proclaimed the Republic of Puerto Rico, offering freedom to the enslaved who joined them; the revolt was crushed within a day and hundreds were imprisoned.
account: Ramón Emeterio Betances and Segundo Ruiz Belvis founded the Revolutionary Committee of Puerto Rico in exile in the Dominican Republic on 6 January 1868. Its cells, organized by Mathias Brugman, Mariana Bracetti and Manuel Rojas, brought together landowners, merchants, professionals, peasants and the enslaved; the economy, slavery and Spanish repression were the catalysts. Betances's arms ship was seized in Saint Thomas, and the plot was discovered in Camuy, so the leaders moved the date forward.

Some 400 to 600 rebels gathered at Manuel Rojas's estate and took Lares around midnight on 23 September 1868. In the church they placed the Lares flag on the altar and proclaimed the Republic of Puerto Rico under Francisco Ramírez Medina, offering freedom to the enslaved who joined them; free blacks burned their libretas. The next morning the rebels were repulsed at San Sebastián del Pepino; four of them died.

Spanish forces arrested more than 800 suspects; some 475 rebels were imprisoned in Arecibo, where they were tortured and humiliated, and on 17 November a military court sentenced them all to death, though they were later amnestied. The revolt failed, but Spain granted more political autonomy. The Lares flag is recognized as the first flag of Puerto Rico.

events.title: The Ten Years' War and the Protest of Baraguá
events.summary: On 10 October 1868 Carlos Manuel de Céspedes freed his slaves and proclaimed Cuba's independence, beginning a ten-year war; at its end Antonio Maceo refused, in the Protest of Baraguá, a peace that neither freed Cuba nor abolished slavery.
account: In the early morning of 10 October 1868 the sugar-mill owner Carlos Manuel de Céspedes issued the cry of independence at La Demajagua, freed his slaves and asked them to join the struggle, calling on men of all races to fight. It was the first of Cuba's three wars of liberation against Spain. Céspedes was killed by a Spanish patrol on 27 February 1874. Spain sent more troops after 1876, until they numbered more than 250,000.

The Pact of Zanjón of 10 February 1878 ended most of the fighting; its most significant reform was freedom for the enslaved who had fought on either side. Antonio Maceo and other Mambises met General Martínez Campos at Los Mangos de Baraguá on 15 March 1878 and rejected it, because it won neither independence nor the abolition of slavery. Maceo fled to Jamaica in May, and hostilities ended on 28 May 1878.
Losses are estimated at 50,000 dead on the Cuban side and 81,248 Spanish dead, 75,000 of them from disease.

events.title: The Moret Law: free wombs in Cuba and Puerto Rico
events.summary: The Moret Law of 4 July 1870 freed children born to enslaved mothers after 18 September 1868, the elderly and those who served Spain, beginning a gradual abolition in Cuba and Puerto Rico while owners were compensated.
account: After the U.S. Civil War, international pressure pushed Spain to end slavery in its last American colonies. The Moret Law, named after Segismundo Moret, Spain's Minister of Overseas Territories, was approved on 4 July 1870 for Cuba and later Puerto Rico; Spain also passed it hoping to preempt the independence movements.

It freed children born to enslaved mothers after 18 September 1868, and children under 14 were not to be separated from their mothers. It also freed the enslaved who served in the Spanish army, those over 60 and those owned by the government. The Spanish government compensated owners 125 pesetas for each person freed. Slavery was abolished in Puerto Rico, but not in Cuba, in 1873, and without exceptions in 1886.

events.title: Slavery ends in Cuba: the patronato and the decree of 1886
events.summary: In 1880 Spain abolished slavery in Cuba gradually, binding the freed to work for their former masters for years at wages too low to live on; slavery was finally abolished by royal decree on 7 October 1886, making Cuba one of the last places in the hemisphere to end it.
account: In 1880 the Spanish legislature abolished slavery in Cuba in a form of gradual abolition: the law required the enslaved to continue to work for their masters for a number of years, in a kind of indentured servitude, for wages so low the freed could barely support themselves.

Slavery was abolished by Spanish royal decree on 7 October 1886, ahead of the schedule of 1888 promised at Zanjón, making Cuba one of the last countries in the Western Hemisphere, before only Brazil, to abolish it. Former slaves joined the ranks of farmers and the urban working class. More than 100,000 Chinese indentured workers had been brought in to replace African labour, and slave traders turned to other sources such as the Indians of Yucatán.

account: Arturo Alfonso Schomburg (24 January 1874 – 10 June 1938) was born in Santurce to Mary Joseph, a freeborn black midwife from St. Croix, and a merchant of German descent. He moved to New York in 1891, joined the Revolutionary Committee of Puerto Rico and in 1892 co-founded Las Dos Antillas, a club for the independence of Cuba and Puerto Rico. He became an important figure of the Harlem Renaissance.

In 1926 the New York Public Library's 135th Street branch bought his private collection of more than 4,000 books for $10,000, funded by the Carnegie Corporation; it became the basis of the Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture in Harlem.

events.title: Cuba's War of Independence and Weyler's reconcentration camps
events.summary: Cuba's last war against Spain began on 24 February 1895; to cut the rebels off from the people, General Valeriano Weyler forced the rural population into fortified towns, where at least 170,000 Cubans, about one in ten, died of disease and hunger.
account: The insurrection organized by José Martí and Máximo Gómez began on 24 February 1895. Martí was killed soon after landing, on 19 May 1895 at Dos Ríos, but Gómez and Antonio Maceo carried the war across the island, reaching its western tip on 22 January 1896. Maceo, the 'Bronze Titan', was killed on 7 December 1896 in Havana province. Spain sent 220,285 soldiers to Cuba, the largest army to cross the Atlantic until World War II.

General Valeriano Weyler answered with periodic executions, mass exile, the destruction of farms and crops, and the reconcentration policy: rural Cubans had eight days to move into camps in fortified towns, and all who failed to obey were to be shot. Housing was decaying, food scarce and disease spread; by 1898 a third of the population had been moved into the camps. Historian John Lawrence Tone estimates that 155,000 to 170,000 civilians died, nearly 10% of the population; the policy is remembered as the first construction of modern concentration camps.

account: The protests began on 11 July 2021, triggered by shortages of food and medicine and the government's response to the resurgent pandemic; they were the largest anti-government demonstrations since the Maleconazo of 1994. The economy had contracted by 10.9% in 2020; causes cited include reduced Venezuelan support, the U.S. embargo and sanctions tightened by the Trump administration in 2019, and the pandemic's blow to tourism and remittances.

One person was confirmed dead in a clash with police; a dissident organization estimated five deaths. The government made hundreds of arrests and charged at least 710 Cubans, some with sedition, giving some long sentences; the United States imposed new sanctions on Cuban officials.

events.title: The great Cuban exodus of 2021–2023
events.place: Cuba; the Mexico–United States border; South Florida
events.summary: Between 2021 and 2023 Cubans left their island in the largest emigration in its history, mostly through Central America and Mexico to the U.S. border and by sea to Florida; estimates run from nearly 500,000 to more than 850,000 people.
account: Driven by economic hardship and political uncertainty, a surge of Cubans left for the United States from 2021, crossing at the Mexico–United States border and arriving by sea in South Florida. It has been described as the largest mass emigration in Cuba's history.

One estimate is that more than 850,000 Cubans sought refuge in the United States between 2021 and 2023, depleting the population by nearly 8%, half of them settling in Miami-Dade County; another gives nearly 500,000, about 5% of the population, with 60% in Miami-Dade.

events.title: Cuba's blackouts and the U.S. fuel blockade
events.summary: From 2024 Cuba's failing power plants and fuel shortages brought repeated blackouts, including a total nationwide blackout from 18 October 2024; in February 2026 the United States began blocking oil tankers bound for Cuba, its first effective blockade since 1962, and by May 2026 Cuba said it had run out of oil and diesel.
account: Blackouts began in February 2024, affecting 45% of the country on 13 February; in March outages of up to 18 hours a day brought protests in Santiago de Cuba. From 18 October 2024 a total nationwide blackout followed the failure of the Antonio Guiteras power plant in Matanzas, the largest. Blackouts continued through 2025 and into 2026, attributed to fuel and spare-part shortages, failing plants and, by some, the U.S. embargo.

In February 2026 the United States began blocking oil tankers heading to Cuba, targeting companies such as Mexico's Pemex; The New York Times called it the first effective U.S. blockade of Cuba since the Missile Crisis. On 13 March 2026 Miguel Díaz-Canel confirmed talks with the United States over the blockade, which had left Cuba with crippling fuel shortages and widespread outages; Cuba released 51 political prisoners and, on 3 April, more than 2,000 prisoners. On 14 May 2026 Cuba's energy ministry warned that the country had run out of oil and diesel.
